title: Housing Outlook Q3 2026
gist: Resolution Foundation quantifies the trade-off behind Andy Burnham's pledge to put council housing at the centre of government: ring-fencing the entire GBP 39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme for social rent would deliver just under 25,000 affordable homes a year versus a 30,000 target, costing 5,100 homes annually, offset only partly by tilting Section 106 toward affordable rent (+2,000/yr) and the National Housing Bank's GBP 2.5 billion 0.1 percent loan facility (+3,700 to 6,100/yr). The net result is 30,000 social rent homes a year against 9,000 recently, but total affordable supply barely moves to 66,000 -- far short of the post-war benchmark -- while Local Housing Allowance, frozen since April 2024, has opened a gap to 30th-percentile rents already above 20 percent and heading for a record this autumn.

insights.claim: Ring-fencing the entire GBP 39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme for social rent would deliver just under 25,000 affordable homes annually against the current target of 30,000, because social rent homes generate lower lifetime rental income and therefore require more upfront grant per unit.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Quantifies the volume cost of tenure politics -- housebuilders and housing association bond issuers should model unit output falling even as the social rent headline rises.
insights.locator: We estimate if all of the Government’s £39 billion grant programme

insights.claim: All homes cost the same to build regardless of final tenure, so the binding variable in affordable housing output is grant per unit rather than construction cost -- meaning tenure policy directly determines volume with the money held fixed.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for forecasting UK affordable completions from any announced funding envelope: divide by the tenure-weighted grant rate, not by build cost.
insights.quote: All homes cost the same amount to build regardless of their final tenure, but because social rent homes offer housing associations a lower lifetime rental income than other affordable products, they require more grant funding upfront
insights.locator: The Burnham government starts from a strong place

insights.claim: Allocating all GBP 39 billion of SAHP funding to social rent would deliver just under 250,000 homes by 2036 -- 50,000 fewer affordable homes overall in the next decade than the programme's 300,000 target.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A 17 percent output haircut is the price of the tenure shift -- the number to hold any government affordable-housing claim against.
insights.locator: If all the £39 billion SAHP funding were allocated to social rent

insights.claim: Reaching 300,000 social rent homes -- the SAHP's total affordable target -- would require another GBP 800 million each year over the programme's 10-year lifespan.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A specific GBP 8 billion cumulative fiscal ask; watch whether it appears in the Budget as the test of whether the council housing pledge is real.
insights.locator: To reach 300,000 homes for social rent

insights.claim: The SAHP, at GBP 39 billion targeting 300,000 affordable homes over 2026-2036, is the largest grant programme since 2011 and expects at least 60 percent to be social rent -- a sharp shift from its predecessor, which had no social rent target and funded just 29 percent social rent between 2021 and March 2025.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: The tenure mix has already shifted before any new announcement -- much of Burnham's stated ambition is inherited policy, limiting incremental upside for suppliers.
insights.locator: The most direct way that central government supports

themes.theme: Section 106 in a weak sales market

insights.claim: Section 106 developer contributions have overtaken grant as the main route to affordable housing in England: between 2015-16 and 2024-25 private developers contributed 244,000 homes, 45 percent of the 542,000 total, against 210,000 supported by grant funding.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Affordable housing supply is now more sensitive to private housebuilding volumes than to Treasury grant -- a cyclical rather than fiscal dependency.
insights.locator: Since the early 2000s, Section 106 agreements have become

insights.claim: In the current market the correct move is to push Section 106 the opposite way from the political direction -- lowering social rent expectations in exchange for a higher number of affordable rent homes, because effective private demand is very weak.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A recommendation that cuts against the government's own rhetoric; if adopted it is a direct cash-flow positive for volume housebuilders.
insights.quote: rather than push Section 106 further towards delivering social rent, there is a strong case to push it the other way
insights.locator: But, just as with grant funding, using Section 106 obligations

insights.claim: Selling a higher number of homes upfront to a housing association does not change a developer's bottom line but does help cash flow and lender confidence at a time when it is taking longer to sell homes on the open market.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Bulk affordable sales are functioning as working-capital relief for UK housebuilders -- a signal that open-market absorption rates, not margins, are the current constraint.
insights.locator: Effective demand in the private market is currently very weak

insights.claim: Only 12 per cent of Section 106 homes over the past five years were built for social rent; converting all of those to affordable rent instead would have produced another 10,000 affordable homes, around 2,000 a year.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Bounds the upside from the Section 106 lever -- useful but not game-changing, which caps how much of the pledge can be delivered without new money.
insights.locator: In the past five years, 12 per cent of Section 106 homes

insights.claim: Pivoting Section 106 toward affordable rent is most effective only when and where private demand is weak, and should not become the long-term norm.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Frames the lever as explicitly cyclical -- policy support for housebuilder cash flow should be expected to reverse when the sales market recovers.
insights.locator: And pivoting Section 106 towards affordable rent

themes.theme: National Housing Bank as subsidy leverage

insights.claim: The newly established National Housing Bank holds a facility to allocate up to GBP 2.5 billion of loans at a 0.1 per cent interest rate repaid after 25 years to housing associations by 2029.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Near-zero-cost 25-year money is a material change to housing association development appraisals -- watch bid volumes as the read on sector development appetite.
insights.locator: In terms of affordable housing, the NHB has a facility

insights.claim: Every GBP 1 of loan on the National Housing Bank's terms is equivalent to 70p of grant, because at an assumed 5 per cent market interest rate the present value of a 0.1 per cent loan repaid after 25 years is only 30p on the pound.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A concrete grant-equivalence formula -- it makes soft-loan facilities directly comparable to grant, and shows how governments can raise output without new grant scoring.
insights.locator: With every £1 of loan offered on the NHB’s terms

insights.claim: The GBP 2.5 billion NHB loan pot could support 11,200 homes if all social rent, 18,400 if all affordable rent, or 13,500 additional affordable homes at the SAHP's planned tenure mix.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A 64 percent output spread between tenure choices for the same capital -- the sharpest illustration of how tenure policy, not funding size, sets volumes.
insights.locator: we estimate the £2.5 billion of loans currently available

insights.claim: The NHB facility is new and untested: the bank only launched in April 2026 and housing associations cannot yet bid for loans, since bids are only possible after initial SAHP grant allocations are made.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Execution risk and sequencing delay mean NHB-driven completions land late in the Parliament, not near term -- do not front-load it in supply forecasts.
insights.locator: But this is a new and untested facility

insights.claim: Allocating more funds to the National Housing Bank loan pot would still cost against the fiscal rules, so soft loans are not a free route to higher affordable supply.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Caps how far the loan channel can be scaled -- fiscal headroom, not institutional design, remains the constraint on UK housing investment.
insights.locator: If those bids offer value for money

themes.theme: Council delivery capacity has been hollowed out

insights.claim: English councils themselves built just 2,000 homes a year in the five years to 2025, against a post-war peak of over 150,000 homes a year, and local authority building ground to a halt in the late 1980s.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A 75x capacity gap makes any council-led delivery pledge implausible on a Parliament timescale -- the delivery will fall to housing associations regardless of rhetoric.
insights.locator: Councils themselves built just 2,000 homes a year

insights.claim: England has never built more than 300,000 homes a year -- the level implied by Labour's 1.5 million homes manifesto target -- without local authorities playing a major role, and the private sector never filled the void: it built on average just 138,000 homes a year in the mid-2000s boom and 128,000 in the late 2010s despite low interest rates and Help to Buy.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Historically, private housebuilding has a hard ceiling around 130-140k a year regardless of demand-side stimulus -- a structural cap that should temper volume expectations for listed builders.
insights.locator: On the one hand, history tells us that England

insights.claim: Two distinct obstacles stand between councils and building at scale: developing in-house expertise after 40 years of not building at scale, and finding additional money.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Capacity rebuilding is a multi-year lead item -- creates demand for development consultancy and project management services before any bricks are laid.
insights.locator: On the other hand, for local authorities to build more homes

insights.claim: Social rent output collapsed over three decades: an average of 42,000 social rent homes were built each year in the 1990s, 79 per cent of the affordable total, but only 78,000 were built in the past ten years combined, equal to 14 per cent of affordable output and a volume the 1990s achieved in under two years.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Shows the tenure shift was driven by grant cuts, with affordable rent substituting to keep headline numbers up -- a template for how funding cuts get disguised.
insights.locator: In the 1990s, an average of 42,000 social rent homes

themes.theme: Net effect: social rent up, total supply flat

insights.claim: Pulling all three levers together could deliver 30,000 social rent homes a year -- a significant boost on the 9,000 delivered annually in the past five years -- while total affordable supply reaches only 66,000 a year, rivalling the mid-1990s but far below the post-war era when local authorities alone built 100,000 homes a year.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: The realistic ceiling under current funding: a tripling of social rent with essentially flat total supply, meaning no incremental volume tailwind for materials or contractors.
insights.locator: pushing grant even further towards social rent

insights.claim: The arithmetic nets out narrowly positive: Section 106 tilting adds around 2,000 homes a year and the National Housing Bank 3,700 to 6,100, together just outweighing the 5,100 annual loss from ring-fencing SAHP funding for social rent.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: The whole policy package is roughly supply-neutral -- treat announcements of a housebuilding boom as tenure reallocation until new money appears.
insights.locator: Together, these gains outweigh the cost of ring-fencing

insights.claim: The stated ambition of the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period would require significantly more money, especially if local authorities building just 2,000 homes a year are to be at the helm.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Sets a clear falsifiable test for the Budget: no substantial new housing money means the pledge is rhetorical.
insights.locator: But this is still a far cry from the “biggest council house building programme

insights.claim: Shifting the SAHP's aims risks undermining progress already made by housing associations that have submitted funding bids to the programme, so the lever cannot be pulled cleanly mid-programme.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Policy-change risk sits directly on housing association development pipelines -- a credit consideration for sector bond investors.
insights.locator: And whatever the lever, all should be pulled cautiously

themes.theme: Housing support gap for private renters

insights.claim: Local Housing Allowance has been frozen since April 2024, when it was pegged to the 30th percentile rent level in the 12 months to September 2023, and the average gap between the help available and the actual 30th percentile has already passed 20 per cent and will reach record levels this autumn.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: A widening 20-plus percent shortfall is a live fiscal and political pressure point for the Budget, and a driver of arrears risk for private landlords.
insights.locator: In the meantime, the support provided to lower-income private renters

insights.claim: Just under a million households -- 950,000 -- receiving Universal Credit in Britain already pay a rent above their Local Housing Allowance and cannot wait a decade for social housing to be built.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Sizes the constituency for an LHA re-peg at the Budget -- a near-term, high-probability spending measure distinct from the long-lead housing programme.
insights.locator: Just under a million households (950,000)

insights.claim: Housing need indicators are at or near record highs in England: a near-record 134,000 households living in temporary accommodation, 1.3 million households on local authority housing waiting lists -- the highest since 2014 -- and private renters spending on average more than a third of their income on housing costs.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: Temporary accommodation costs are a direct and rising local authority budget liability -- a driver of council financial distress independent of the building programme.
insights.locator: His commitment to boosting the number of affordable homes is welcome

insights.claim: The term council housing as used politically is ambiguous, spanning affordable rent at around 80 per cent of market rate, shared ownership, and social rent at roughly 50 per cent of market rate -- and the colloquial meaning is social rent regardless of whether councils or housing associations own the homes.
insights.speaker: Hannah Aldridge
insights.so_what: The definitional ambiguity is where delivery shortfalls will be hidden; the 50 percent versus 80 percent market-rate distinction determines the actual subsidy bill.
insights.locator: The phrase is ambiguous
